prompts.text: What sort of creative work makes you stop and look twice, even when you don't know much about it?
Enjoying a painting doesn't require explaining what the artist intended.
We're at an exhibition and choose completely different favourite pieces. How would you defend your pick?
Trying pottery with uneven results or learning to draw simple portraits of each other?
Tell me about something you made with your hands and felt quietly pleased to finish.
Watching someone concentrate on a small creative project is often more interesting than seeing the result.
Have you seen a piece of public art which changed how you looked at a familiar street?
An imperfect handmade object often has a better story than a polished shop-bought one.
I bring a sketchbook and ask you to draw the first thing you notice. What lands on the page?
A gallery with a handful of unusual pieces or a busy craft market full of handmade things?
Which app do you enjoy using, and which one steals more of your time than you intend?
Putting a phone away during a conversation feels better when nobody makes a formal rule about it.
We both forget our chargers on a long train ride. What would we end up talking about first?
A day with no social media or a day with no streaming services?
Tell me about something interesting you found while looking for something completely different online.
People sometimes remember the comments under a video longer than the video itself.
What's a piece of technology you wish still worked as simply as it did years ago?
Sharing funny things online works best when you understand the other person's sense of humour.
I show you a strange photo from my camera roll with no explanation. What's your first question?
Printing a few favourite photos or keeping a carefully organised digital album?
What's a question you've asked recently because you genuinely wanted to know the answer?
A good explanation leaves room for someone to ask a second question without feeling embarrassed.
We join a beginner's workshop where neither of us knows what we're doing. Who asks for help first?
Learning a few phrases in a new language or figuring out how an everyday object is made?
Tell me about a fact you learnt by accident and still bring up in conversations.
Some interesting conversations begin with somebody admitting they don't know something.
If you had a free afternoon with an expert in any field, what would you ask them to show you?
Curiosity is more enjoyable when you don't turn every interesting topic into homework.
We're at a science museum and one exhibit has a queue. What would persuade you to wait?
A hands-on lesson where you make mistakes or a relaxed talk where you leave with new questions?
When did a stranger last make an ordinary errand easier for you?
A polite gesture matters more when someone does it without expecting attention.
We're carrying shopping bags and notice somebody struggling with a heavy door. What happens next?
Receiving a thoughtful handwritten note or hearing someone mention a kind thing you did weeks ago?
Tell me about a time you were unexpectedly grateful for someone's patience.
A brief exchange with a stranger sometimes improves your mood for the rest of the day.
What's a simple way someone shows respect which you notice immediately?
Being considerate is easier when you ask what helps instead of assuming you already know.
I realise the café has given me somebody else's order. Would you return it straight away or ask the staff for help?
Helping someone find their way around a new place or lending a useful item when they need it?
What's something people do in queues which always catches your attention?
Ordinary conversations overheard on public transport sometimes sound like the start of a novel.
We notice two strangers wearing almost identical outfits. Do you point it out or keep the observation to yourself?
Watching a busy market wake up in the morning or seeing a quiet street come alive after work?
Tell me about a harmless misunderstanding in public which turned into a funny story.
You learn a lot about a place by noticing what people stop to look at.
What's a tiny detail in restaurants or cafés which you notice before most people do?
A little people-watching is more fun when you're curious rather than judgemental.
We're waiting for a bus when someone starts an impromptu street performance. Would you stop to watch?
Sitting by a window overlooking a lively street or finding a bench with an uninterrupted view of the sky?
